title: Don't Make Hints Unavoidable
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton uses this Tips for Teachers entry to argue that hints and cues, however well-intended, can quietly sabotage retrieval practice when they are built into the task itself. He starts from the premise that the most powerful retrieval happens with no cues present, because that mirrors the conditions of an exam, while conceding that students who cannot recall anything gain little from staring at a blank page. Using a Do Now he saw on a school visit, where red hints sat beside the first three questions, he shows how students who did not need help were robbed of the chance to find out what they could retrieve independently. He extends the point to verbal reminders and visual cues such as underlined key words, which he sees routinely in classrooms. His remedy is to keep hints available but avoidable: on the back of the sheet, revealed after a delay, or delivered privately to the students identified as needing them while circulating.
points: Barton grounds the tip in retrieval research: cue-free recall is the strongest form of retrieval because it matches the unaided conditions students face in exams.
He accepts that hints are sometimes necessary to kick-start retrieval for students who genuinely cannot recall, so the issue is when and to whom hints are given, not whether they exist.
Hints printed alongside questions are 'unavoidable' and remove the retrieval opportunity for every student, including those who could have succeeded unaided.
The same problem appears in whole-class verbal hints ('do the same to both sides') and visual cues such as underlining key words before students begin.
His fix is to make hints available but hidden: on the back of the paper, revealed after five minutes, or given individually to students identified while circulating.
quotes: The most powerful form of retrieval is when there are no hints or cues present. All students have available are their own memories, which is all they will have in an exam.

However, if students cannot recall the knowledge they need, there is little point in them staring at a blank page for the duration of the retrieval opportunity. Therefore, in such circumstances, it makes sense to offer students hints and cues that might be enough to kick-start the retrieval process.

These hints are great, and allowed students who were struggling with these questions to access them. But what about the students who did not need these hints? Because the hints are unavoidable - as soon as you read the question you see them - they were robbed of an opportunity to see what they could retrieve independently.

I see the same issue play out a lot in the classrooms I visit. Just before students attempt a question, the teacher offers a verbal hint: “Remember to do the same to both sides”, or “Watch out, this one is a bit different to the last question”.

The solution, I think, is to refrain from giving hints and cues so students can see what they can do without them, but have them available when students need them. So, in the Do Now example, the hints could be on the back of the piece of paper, or only revealed on the board after 5 minutes.
